we present a photometric-stereo-based system for the retrieval of the RGB albedo of an opaque surface and the fine-scale 3D-structure of its microgeometry, which is calibrated without demosaicing and which is applicable to a wide variety of materials.

(i) photometric stereo is a powerful technique that can be used for 3D-reconstructing very thin structures from real-world scenes, (ii) a dedicated diffuse lighting calibration is required to avoid specularities, (iii) RAW images can be used to avoid uncontrolled demosaicing, (iv) a simple RGB albedo estimation is possible without the need for a demosaicing step.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new system for the capture of the fine-scale details (e.g., microstructures and textures) of opaque surfaces by means of photometric stereo, which is based on a controllable diffuse lighting, and which does not require demosaicing.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of RAW data and of a controllable diffuse lighting enables the capture of fine-scale details of opaque surfaces, without the need for demosaicing and without the need for a complex illumination setup.

photometric stereo can be successfully used in the presence of strong specularities, and that the system can be easily extended to handle other types of surfaces, such as transparent ones, and other types of sensors.
